sentences.text: Beibeilong was a large, bipedal dinosaur estimated to reach a length of 7.5 meters and a mass between 1.5 and 2 metric tons.
Its jaws were toothless and equipped with a horny beak known as a rhamphotheca, a structure lacking the sockets typically found for teeth.
Some of its neck vertebrae possessed large air-filled hollow depressions on their sides.
The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — is an embryonic skeleton measuring only 23 centimeters from the top of the skull to the base of the tail.
The skull of the Baby Louie specimen has been damaged due to scavenging and erosion.
Beibeilong eggs belong to the oospecies Macroelongatoolithus xixiaensis, which are the largest known type of dinosaur eggs.
The skeleton was popularly known as "Baby Louie" in recognition of Louie Psihoyos, the photographer of the article, and found its final home in the Henan Geological Museum in December 2013.
The generic name Beibeilong means "baby dragon" in Chinese, derived from pinyin where beibei means baby and long means dragon.
Beibeilong was named and described in 2017 based on an embryonic skeleton and partial nest found in Henan Province, China, between 1992 and 1993.
The fossil specimen includes perinate skeletal remains found alongside 2 to 3 eggs.
Beibeilong laid large Macroelongatoolithus eggs measuring 40 to 45 cm in length with ruggedly ornamented shells.
Researchers propose that the adult Beibeilong sat in the center of its egg clutch during incubation to avoid crushing them.
It is debated whether adult oviraptorosaurs found with nests were incubating eggs, laying eggs, or guarding the nest.
Beibeilong is classified as a basal member of the family Caenagnathidae, rather than the oviraptorids.
In 2017, researchers considered Beibeilong to be anatomically similar to but more primitive than Gigantoraptor, and it is not an embryonic individual of that taxon.
Beibeilong lived in China during the Late Cretaceous epoch, specifically the Cenomanian to Coniacian ages, between 100.5 and 89.8 million years ago.
It inhabited humid floodplains with rivers in environments ranging from semi-arid to tropical climates where Araucariaceae conifers were largely present.
Evidence suggests that large oviraptorosaurs like Beibeilong preferred well-watered habitats over desertic ones.
It is debated whether Beibeilong had teeth; some researchers argue for a dietary shift involving lost teeth, while others reject this based on phylogeny suggesting simple dentaries are ancestral.
It is probable that the embryo was forcibly removed or taken from one of the underlying eggs, given that the skeleton is not preserved inside an egg and its orientation is inconsistent with the eggs.
